extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political economy; policymakers interested in colonial/trade policy
extracted.subtask_description: Normative and explanatory principles about colonial representation, the mercantile system, monopolies, and the distribution of capital (stock) in national economies; aimed at assessing policies toward colonies, trade regulation, and chartered companies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation from every part of the empire
rubrics_metrics.description: The assembly which deliberates and decides concerning the affairs of every part of the empire, in order to be properly informed, ought certainly to have representatives from every part of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that a legislature that governs the whole empire must include representatives from all parts so it can be properly informed; this would complete rather than hurt the constitution. Practical difficulties may arise, largely from prejudices, but are not insurmountable. Examples/discussion: fears about American representatives overturning balance; counterargument that proportional representation by taxation/population maintains constitutional balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportional representation by taxation/produce
rubrics_metrics.description: If the number of American representatives were to be in proportion to the produce of American taxation, the number of people to be managed would increase exactly in proportion to the means of managing them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A representative share proportional to contribution (taxation) keeps the monarchical and democratical parts of the constitution in the same relative force; thus representation should reflect fiscal contribution to avoid upsetting constitutional balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative responsibility despite distance
rubrics_metrics.description: The distance could not much weaken the dependency of the representative upon the constituent, and the former would still feel that he owed his seat in parliament ... to the good-will of the latter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remote constituents are protected because their representatives have incentives (re-election, reputation) to complain about outrages and defend them; practical expectation that colonies will grow and move the seat of empire closer in time is also given as mitigation of distance concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seat of empire follows economic contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: The seat of the empire would then naturally remove itself to that part of the empire which contributed most to the general defence and support of the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because colonies may grow rapidly in wealth and population, political center naturally shifts toward the area contributing most to defense and support; a historical/forward-looking argument about imperial dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discoveries tend to unite distant parts beneficially
rubrics_metrics.description: By uniting in some measure the most distant parts of the world, by enabling them to relieve one another’s wants, to increase one another’s enjoyments, and to encourage one another’s industry, their general tendency would seem to be beneficial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The discovery of America and the Cape broaden commerce and communication; though immediate consequences include misfortunes to natives (due to superior force), the long-term tendency of mutual communication and knowledge diffusion is to establish equality of force and mutual respect of rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natives' misfortunes result from imbalance of force, not discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: These misfortunes ... seem to have arisen rather from accident than from any thing in the nature of those events themselves. ... the superiority of force ... enabled [Europeans] to commit ... injustice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The harm to indigenous peoples is attributed to temporary European superiority of force; future equality of force through commerce and knowledge could reduce such injustices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commerce spreads knowledge and equalizes force
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing seems more likely to establish this equality of force, than that mutual communication of knowledge, and of all sorts of improvements, which an extensive commerce from all countries to all countries naturally ... carries along with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensive commerce promotes exchange of knowledge and improvements, which tends to equalize power and restrain interstate injustice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective of the mercantile system
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the object of that system to enrich a great nation, rather by trade and manufactures than by the improvement and cultivation of land, rather by the industry of the towns than by that of the country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discoveries expanded markets and transformed commercial towns into large-scale manufacturers and carriers for the world; mercantile policy therefore focuses on maximizing trade/manufacturing advantage rather than agricultural improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colonies can benefit foreign countries more than the metropole
rubrics_metrics.description: The colonies of Spain and Portugal, for example, give more real encouragement to the industry of other countries than to that of Spain and Portugal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: colonial demand for linen is largely supplied by France, Flanders, Holland, Germany rather than Spain/Portugal themselves; colonial consumption can distribute capital and revenue abroad, leaving the metropole to enjoy only the spent profits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restraints on direct colonial trade harm the imposing country
rubrics_metrics.description: Even the regulations by which each nation endeavours to secure to itself the exclusive trade of its own colonies, are frequently more hurtful to the countries in favour of which they are established, than to those against which they are established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restrictions force indirect trade routes (e.g., Hamburg merchant forced to route via London), increasing costs and slowing returns; some harm returns to the imposing country by misallocating capital and reducing national advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monopoly is the engine of the mercantile system
rubrics_metrics.description: Monopoly is the great engine of both; but it is a different sort of monopoly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two kinds described: (1) exclusive national exclusion of other nations from colonial trade; (2) exclusive companies within a nation (e.g., East India Company). Both derange natural distribution of stock and have different effects depending on circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private interests naturally distribute stock optimally
rubrics_metrics.description: The private interests and passions of individuals naturally lead them to divide and distribute the stock of every society among all the different employments carried on in it; as nearly as possible in the proportion which is most agreeable to the interest of the whole society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capital flows to nearer, more frequently-returning employments; when profits rise in distant employments, stock moves until profits equalize. This market mechanism corrects over- or under-allocation without law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Profit signals correct misallocation of capital
rubrics_metrics.description: If the profit should happen to rise somewhat higher ... this superiority of profit will draw stock ... till the profits of all return to their proper level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High profits in understocked distant employments attract capital away from nearer employments until equilibrium is restored; such profit differences are evidence of under- or over-stocking and of goods being above/below their natural price.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derangements of stock distribution are harmful
rubrics_metrics.description: Every derangement of the natural distribution of stock is necessarily hurtful to the society in which it takes place; whether it be by repelling from a particular trade the stock which would otherwise go to it, or by attracting towards a particular trade that which would not otherwise come to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a country losing potential East India trade suffers loss if company exclusion repels domestic capital; conversely, poor countries may be artificially drawn into distant trade unsuited to their needs. Public interest may require shifting capital contrary to private preference in extraordinary cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monopolies of the first kind attract stock
rubrics_metrics.description: Monopolies of the first kind always attract to the particular trade in which they are established a greater proportion of the stock of the society than what would go to that trade of its own accord.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nationwide exclusionary monopolies push disproportionate capital into the monopolized trade, distorting normal allocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monopolies of the second kind have mixed effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Monopolies of the second kind may sometimes attract stock towards the particular trade in which they are established, and sometimes repel it from that trade, according to different circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In poor countries, exclusive companies encourage adventurers and thus attract capital; in rich countries they may limit capacity and repel capital that would otherwise flow into that trade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive companies can promote trade in poor countries
rubrics_metrics.description: Such poor countries as Sweden and Denmark, for example, would probably have never sent a single ship to the East Indies, had not the trade been subjected to an exclusive company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monopoly companies provide sufficient incentive and certainty of profit to encourage small-capital adventurers, enabling distant trade that otherwise wouldn't occur in poor countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive companies can restrict trade in rich countries
rubrics_metrics.description: The limited stock of the Dutch East India company probably repels from that trade many great mercantile capitals which would otherwise go to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In wealthy nations with abundant capital, imposing exclusive companies can prevent the trade from absorbing otherwise redundant capital, reducing the potential scale of trade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive companies often cause fraud, waste, and higher prices
rubrics_metrics.description: Since the establishment of the English East India company ... the other inhabitants of England ... must have paid ... for all the extraordinary waste which the fraud and abuse inseparable from the management of the affairs of so great a company must necessarily have occasioned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chartered companies' monopoly profits and management inefficiencies are borne by domestic consumers in higher prices; company governance tends toward abuses that reduce national advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: No branch of trade strictly requires an exclusive company
rubrics_metrics.description: This argument, however, if it proved any thing at all, would prove that no one great branch of trade could be carried on without an exclusive company, which is contrary to the experience of all nations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a nation is ripe for a trade, its merchants and capital will divide among principal and subordinate branches naturally; trade can be carried on without single-merchant monopolies or companies, as historical Portuguese experience shows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign interest in increasing annual produce and markets
rubrics_metrics.description: The greater the revenue of the people, therefore, the greater the annual produce of their land and labour, the more they can afford to the sovereign. It is his interest, therefore, to increase as much as possible that annual produce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Therefore sovereigns should open the most extensive market, allow perfect freedom of commerce, abolish monopolies and restraints on transport/export/import to increase production, competition of buyers, and thus sovereign revenue—company mercantile habits conflict with this interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merchant-governed companies prioritize merchant profit over sovereign welfare
rubrics_metrics.description: Trade, or buying in order to sell again, they still consider as their principal business, and by a strange absurdity, regard the character of the sovereign as but an appendix to that of the merchant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Companies that become sovereigns tend to make government subservient to mercantile aims: keeping out competitors, restricting production, and preferring monopolist profits over the long-term revenue that comes from increasing the people's productive capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Company governments may deliberately limit production to protect monopoly
rubrics_metrics.description: In the spice islands, the Dutch are said to burn all the spiceries which a fertile season produces, beyond what they expect to dispose of in Europe ... The best way, they imagine, to secure their own monopoly, is to take care that no more shall grow than what they themselves carry to market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: companies may suppress production, destroy crops, or extirpate plants to maintain high prices and monopoly; such policies are destructive and contrary to public/sovreign interest.
